H&P – Detailed Note

Consult Summary:
35-year-old lawyer with new, intermittent frontal headaches plus palpitations, shortness of breath, arm tingling, 5-lb unintentional weight loss, reduced appetite, and loss of libido since changing to a higher-stress job; plan for in-person assessment and thyroid labs.

History:
• Presenting complaint: Intermittent severe frontal headaches; additional episodes of palpitations, shortness of breath, bilateral arm tingling, decreased appetite, weight loss, and reduced libido.  
• Onset/Timeline: All symptoms began after recent job change (exact date not specified; weeks–months).  
  – Headaches: Frontal; occur during work meetings or computer use; no radiation; occasional mild nausea; no prior headache history.  
  – Palpitations: Sense of fast heart beat ~1×/day, sometimes in elevator or while seated at desk.  
  – Shortness of breath: Episodic while sitting at desk; absent with exercise.  
  – Tingling: “Quick pricking” in both arms; no leg involvement; first occurrence with current illness.  
  – Constitutional: Reduced appetite and unintentional 5-lb weight loss; clothes not noticeably looser; no external comments on weight change.  
  – Loss of libido beginning at same time as other symptoms.  
• Exacerbating factors: Work stress (self-rated 7–8/10), computer work/meetings.  
• Relieving factors: None reported.  
• Pertinent negatives: No headaches on commute; no smoking; no recreational drug use; no tingling in legs; no exercise-induced dyspnea.

Past Medical History:
• Hyperthyroidism (patient-reported).  
  – Current status/complications not discussed.

Medications:
• Thyroxine – dose/route/frequency not documented.  
Allergies: Not documented.

Social History:
• Occupation: Lawyer in London; high work stress (7–8/10).  
• Alcohol: ~2 glasses of wine once/week.  
• Tobacco: Non-smoker.  
• Recreational drugs: Denies use.

Family History:
• Not discussed.

Physical Examination:
• Vitals: Not recorded (tele-consult).  
• Other exam findings: Not recorded.

Investigations:
• Planned: In-clinic physical examination (cardiac and respiratory), blood tests including thyroid function panel.

Assessment & Plan:
Overall Impression:
Multi-system symptoms (headache, palpitations, SOB, paresthesias, weight loss) after job change; possible thyroxine over-replacement causing hyperthyroid picture versus stress/anxiety-related disorder; other etiologies (primary headache disorder) considered.

DDx Integration:
1. Iatrogenic hyperthyroidism (excess thyroxine) – supports: on thyroxine, heat intolerance/“feeling hot,” palpitations, weight loss, libido loss; opposes: no tremor or diarrhea reported.  
2. Stress-related or anxiety/panic disorder – supports: symptoms predominantly at work, high stress rating, episodic palpitations/SOB/tingling; opposes: objective weight loss and heat intolerance less typical.  
3. Primary tension or migraine headaches – supports: frontal headaches with screen work, mild nausea; opposes: does not explain systemic/autonomic symptoms.

Issue 1 – Possible thyroid hormone imbalance  
• Plan:
  – Schedule in-person visit for full physical exam, vitals.  
  – Order thyroid function tests (TSH, free T4, ± free T3) and basic metabolic panel.  
  – Review current thyroxine dose and adherence once labs available.  

Issue 2 – Stress/anxiety-related symptoms  
• Plan:
  – Screen for anxiety/depression at in-person visit.  
  – Discuss workplace stress management, sleep hygiene, regular breaks from screen, relaxation techniques.  
  – Consider referral for cognitive behavioral therapy if symptoms persist after medical causes excluded.

Issue 3 – New-onset headache disorder  
• Plan:
  – Assess red-flag features during physical exam (neurological deficits, papilledema).  
  – If concerning features or abnormal neuro exam, consider neuro-imaging.  
  – Provide interim advice: adequate hydration, ergonomic workstation adjustments, OTC analgesia as needed (dose guidance at visit).

General plan items:  
• Safety net: Advise patient to seek urgent care for severe or worsening headaches, persistent palpitations, syncope, or neurological deficits.  
• Follow-up: Review lab results and symptom status within 2 weeks after in-person assessment.

Quality checks:
• Missing elements: Allergies, family history, medication dose/frequency, vital signs not obtained.  
• No direct conflicts noted between transcript and DDx.  
• Transcript quality: Adequate; occasional pauses and incomplete answers but core data captured.
